title: Rectifiers
description: Turn AC into DC with half-wave and full-wave rectifiers, and smooth the result with a capacitor.

study.title: Half-wave rectifier
study.body: With $v_s = V_m\sin\omega t$, the diode conducts only during the positive half-cycles. With a resistive load the output follows $v_s$ (minus about 0.7 V) when the diode is on, and is zero during the negative half-cycles. Peak output: $V_m - 0.7$ V (or $V_m$ for an ideal diode).

study.title: Smoothing capacitor and ripple
study.body: A capacitor across the load charges to the peak voltage, then supplies the load current $I_L$ while the diode is off, discharging slowly until the next peak. The peak-to-peak **ripple** $V_r$ follows from $Q = I_L T = C V_r$, with $T = 1/f$. The average load voltage is about $V_{peak} - V_r/2$. Drag $C$ (ideal diode, $V_m$ = 10 V): doubling $C$ halves the ripple, because the same charge $I_LT$ is drawn from a larger capacitance.

study.title: Center-tapped full-wave rectifier
study.body: A center-tapped transformer gives two voltages $v_s$ in opposite phase. $D_1$ conducts on one half-cycle, $D_2$ on the other, so the load gets a pulse every half period. Peak output $V_m - 0.7$ V, where $V_m$ is the peak of **each half** of the secondary. The capacitor is recharged twice per cycle:

study.title: Bridge rectifier
study.body: Four diodes; on each half-cycle two of them conduct in series with the load, so no center tap is needed. Here $D_2$ and $D_3$ conduct when the right side of the source is positive, $D_1$ and $D_4$ when the left side is. Peak output: $V_m - 1.4$ V (two diode drops). Ripple as for any full-wave rectifier: $V_r \approx I_L T/(2C)$.

study.title: Peak inverse voltage (PIV)
study.body:
The PIV is the largest reverse voltage a diode sees; the diode's breakdown voltage must exceed it. With ideal diodes:
- Half-wave, resistive load: $V_m$
- Half-wave with smoothing capacitor: about $2V_m$ (capacitor holds $+V_m$ while the source swings to $-V_m$)
- Center-tapped full-wave: $2V_m$
- Bridge: $V_m$

study.title: Design recipe
study.body:
- Load current $I_L = V_L/R_L$.
- Pick the ripple $V_r$; then $C = I_L T/V_r$ (half-wave) or $C = I_L T/(2V_r)$ (full-wave).
- Required source peak: $V_m = V_{L,avg} + V_r/2 +$ diode drops (0.7 V half-wave or center-tap, 1.4 V bridge).
- Transformer rating: $V_{rms} = V_m/\sqrt{2}$.
**Example:** bridge, $V_L$ = 12 V avg, $V_r$ = 1 V: $V_m$ = 12 + 0.5 + 1.4 = 13.9 V.

steps.title: The half-wave rectifier
steps.body: The source is $v_s = V_m\sin\omega t$. During positive half-cycles the diode is forward biased and $v_o \approx v_s - 0.7$ V. During negative half-cycles it is reverse biased and blocks.

steps.prompt: In the half-wave rectifier with a resistive load, what is $v_o$ during the negative half-cycles of $v_s$?
steps.explanation: During the negative half-cycle the anode is below the cathode, so the diode is off. No current flows through $R_L$, so $v_o = 0$ and the whole source voltage appears across the diode.

steps.prompt: A half-wave rectifier with a resistive load is driven by $v_s$ = {{Vm}} sin(ωt) V. Using the 0.7 V diode model, find the peak output voltage.
steps.explanation:
At the positive peak the diode conducts and drops 0.7 V:
$V_{o,peak} = V_m - 0.7$ = {{Vm}} − 0.7 = {{Vm-0.7|V}}.

steps.title: Smoothing with a capacitor
steps.body: A capacitor across the load charges to the peak, then feeds the load while the diode is off. The output now only dips a little before the next peak: that dip is the **ripple** $V_r$ (peak to peak). The capacitor supplies charge $I_L T$ per cycle, so $CV_r \approx I_L T$.

steps.prompt: A half-wave rectifier at {{f}} Hz with a {{C|F}} smoothing capacitor supplies a load current of {{IL|A}}. Estimate the peak-to-peak ripple voltage.
steps.explanation: $T = 1/f$ = {{1/f|s}}. Half-wave: $V_r \approx \frac{I_L T}{C} = \frac{ {{IL}}\times{{1/f}} }{ {{C}} }$ = {{IL/(f*C)|V}}.

steps.prompt: For the same load current, a larger smoothing capacitor gives a smaller ripple.
steps.explanation: $V_r \approx I_L T/C$: the capacitor loses the same charge $I_L T$ each cycle, and a larger $C$ means a smaller voltage drop for that charge.

steps.title: Full-wave rectifiers
steps.body: Full-wave rectifiers use **both** half-cycles. The **center-tapped** version uses two diodes and a transformer with a center tap; the **bridge** uses four diodes, two of which conduct in series on each half-cycle (peak output $V_m - 1.4$ V). The capacitor is recharged twice per cycle, so the ripple halves: $V_r \approx I_L T/(2C)$.

steps.prompt: Match each rectifier with its description
pairs: One diode, conducts on half of each cycle
Two diodes and a center-tapped transformer
Four diodes, two conducting at a time
steps.explanation: The half-wave rectifier wastes the negative half-cycles. Both full-wave types use the whole cycle: the center-tapped one needs a special transformer but only one diode drop; the bridge needs no center tap but has two diode drops in the current path.

steps.prompt: A full-wave rectifier runs from the {{f}} Hz mains. What is the frequency of the ripple on its output?
steps.explanation: The capacitor is recharged on every half-cycle, i.e. twice per period, so the ripple repeats at $2f$ = {{2*f}} Hz. (For a half-wave rectifier it would be {{f}} Hz.)

steps.prompt: Bridge rectifier. During the half cycle in which the **top** terminal of the source is positive, tap the diodes that conduct.
steps.explanation: Follow the current out of the + terminal (top): it reaches the left corner, where only $D_1$ points away from it, up to the top corner. From there it flows down through $R_L$ to the bottom corner, through $D_3$ to the right corner and back into the source's bottom terminal. $D_2$ and $D_4$ are reverse biased. Two diodes conduct in series, so the output peak is about $V_m - 1.4$ V.

steps.prompt: A bridge rectifier with a resistive load is driven by $v_s$ = {{Vm}} sin(ωt) V. Using the 0.7 V diode model, find the peak load voltage.
steps.explanation:
On each half-cycle the current passes through **two** diodes in series with the load (e.g. $D_2$ and $D_3$):
$V_{L,peak} = V_m - 2(0.7)$ = {{Vm}} − 1.4 = {{Vm-1.4|V}}.

steps.prompt: A 60 Hz half-wave rectifier ($V_m$ = {{Vm|V}}, 0.7 V diode) feeds $R_L$ = {{RL|Ω}} in parallel with $C$ = {{C|F}}. Estimate the ripple, using the peak load voltage to find $I_L$.
steps.explanation:
$I_L \approx (V_m - 0.7)/R_L = {{Vm-0.7}}/{{RL}}$ = {{IL|A}}.
$V_r \approx \frac{I_L T}{C} = \frac{ {{IL}} }{60\times{{C}} }$ = {{IL/(60*C)|V}}.

steps.prompt: A full-wave rectifier at {{f}} Hz must supply {{IL|A}} with at most {{Vr|V}} peak-to-peak ripple. What capacitance is needed?
steps.explanation:
Full-wave: $V_r \approx \frac{I_L T}{2C}$, so
$C = \frac{I_L T}{2V_r} = \frac{ {{IL}} }{2\times{{f}}\times{{Vr}} }$ = {{IL/(2*f*Vr)|F}}.

steps.prompt: A bridge rectifier with a smoothing capacitor has $V_m$ = {{Vm|V}} and a ripple of {{Vr|V}} peak to peak. Using the 0.7 V model, estimate the average load voltage.
steps.explanation:
The capacitor charges to $V_m - 1.4$ = {{Vm-1.4|V}} and sags by $V_r$, so the average is about halfway:
$V_{L,avg} \approx V_m - 1.4 - V_r/2$ = {{Vm-1.4-Vr/2|V}}.

steps.prompt: In a center-tapped full-wave rectifier, each half of the secondary has a peak voltage of {{Vm|V}}. What is the peak inverse voltage across each (ideal) diode?
steps.explanation: When $D_1$ conducts, the output (cathode of $D_2$) is at $+V_m$ while the anode of $D_2$ is at $-V_m$ (the other end of the secondary). So $D_2$ sees $2V_m$ = {{2*Vm|V}} in reverse.

steps.prompt: A bridge rectifier is driven by a source with peak {{Vm|V}}. Treating the diodes as ideal, what is the peak inverse voltage across each diode?
steps.explanation: When $D_2$ and $D_3$ conduct (ideal, so 0 V), each of $D_1$ and $D_4$ is connected directly across the source in reverse. The PIV is $V_m$ = {{Vm|V}}: half of what the center-tapped circuit needs.

steps.prompt: A transformer secondary is rated {{Vrms}} V rms and feeds a bridge rectifier with a resistive load. Using the 0.7 V model, find the peak load voltage.
steps.explanation:
The peak of a sinusoid is $\sqrt{2}$ times its rms value: $V_m = \sqrt{2}\times{{Vrms}}$ = {{sqrt(2)*Vrms|V}}.
Subtract two diode drops: {{sqrt(2)*Vrms}} − 1.4 = {{sqrt(2)*Vrms-1.4|V}}.

steps.prompt: For the same load current and capacitor, a full-wave rectifier has about half the ripple of a half-wave rectifier.
steps.explanation: The full-wave rectifier recharges the capacitor every $T/2$ instead of every $T$, so it only has to supply the load for half as long: $V_r \approx I_L T/(2C)$ versus $I_L T/C$.

steps.prompt: Bridge rectifier. During the half cycle in which the **bottom** terminal of the source is positive, tap the diodes that conduct.
steps.explanation: Now the current leaves the bottom terminal and runs around to the right corner. $D_4$ carries it to the top corner, it flows down through $R_L$ (in the **same** direction as in the other half cycle) and returns through $D_2$ to the left corner and the source's top terminal. $D_1$ and $D_3$ are reverse biased. That is the point of the bridge: $R_L$ always sees current from top to bottom, so both half cycles are used.

steps.prompt: A half-wave rectifier with a smoothing capacitor must give an **average** load voltage of {{VL|V}} with {{Vr|V}} peak-to-peak ripple. Using the 0.7 V model, what source peak $V_m$ is needed?
steps.explanation:
The load voltage peaks at $V_{L,avg} + V_r/2$ = {{VL+Vr/2|V}}, and the diode drops 0.7 V on top of that:
$V_m = {{VL}} + {{Vr/2}} + 0.7$ = {{VL+Vr/2+0.7|V}}.

steps.prompt: The same half-wave supply at {{f}} Hz delivers {{IL|A}} with {{Vr|V}} ripple. What smoothing capacitance does it need?
steps.explanation:
Half-wave: $C = \frac{I_L T}{V_r} = \frac{ {{IL}} }{ {{f}}\times{{Vr}} }$ = {{IL/(f*Vr)|F}}.
A full-wave circuit would need only half: {{IL/(2*f*Vr)|F}}.

steps.prompt: A **bridge** rectifier with a smoothing capacitor must give an average load voltage of {{VL|V}} with {{Vr|V}} ripple. Using the 0.7 V model, what source peak $V_m$ is needed?
steps.explanation:
Peak load voltage $V_{L,avg} + V_r/2$ = {{VL+Vr/2|V}}, plus **two** diode drops in a bridge:
$V_m = {{VL+Vr/2}} + 1.4$ = {{VL+Vr/2+1.4|V}}.

steps.prompt: A bridge rectifier at {{f}} Hz feeds a {{RL|Ω}} load at about {{VL|V}}. Find the capacitance for a ripple of {{Vr|V}}.
steps.explanation:
$I_L = V_L/R_L = {{VL}}/{{RL}}$ = {{IL|A}}.
Full-wave: $C = \frac{I_L T}{2V_r} = \frac{ {{IL}} }{2\times{{f}}\times{{Vr}} }$ = {{IL/(2*f*Vr)|F}}.

steps.prompt: A half-wave rectifier with a large smoothing capacitor and a light load is driven by a {{Vm|V}} peak source. What is the approximate peak inverse voltage across the (ideal) diode?
steps.explanation: The capacitor stays charged near $+V_m$ (cathode side). At the negative peak the anode is at $-V_m$, so the diode sees $V_m - (-V_m) = 2V_m$ = {{2*Vm|V}}. Without the capacitor the PIV would be only $V_m$.

steps.prompt: A center-tapped full-wave supply must give an average {{VL|V}} with {{Vr|V}} ripple. Using the 0.7 V model, what rms voltage must **each half** of the secondary provide?
steps.explanation:
Only one diode is in the current path: $V_m = V_{L,avg} + V_r/2 + 0.7$ = {{Vm|V}}.
Each half of the secondary: $V_{rms} = V_m/\sqrt{2}$ = {{Vm/sqrt(2)|V}} (so {{2*Vm/sqrt(2)|V}} rms end to end).

steps.prompt: Put the steps of designing a capacitor-filtered rectifier supply in order
items: Find the required peak $V_m$ including $V_r/2$ and the diode drops
Check the diode PIV and current ratings
steps.explanation: The load sets $I_L$; with the allowed ripple that gives $C$. The ripple and diode drops then set how large the source peak must be, which fixes the transformer. Finally make sure the diodes can withstand the PIV.

steps.prompt: The source voltage is a sine wave. Which graph shows the load voltage of a **full-wave** rectifier with a resistive load (no capacitor)? All graphs use the same axes.
steps.explanation: A full-wave rectifier passes the positive half-cycles and **flips** the negative ones, so the load sees $|v_s|$: two positive humps per period. A half-wave rectifier leaves gaps of zero during the negative half-cycles; the plain sine is the unrectified source, and the slowly sagging waveform needs a smoothing capacitor.

steps.prompt: The graph shows the output of a rectifier with a smoothing capacitor, fed from a {{f}} Hz source. Which kind of rectifier is it?

curves.f: max(Vp*((2-m)*max(0, sin(w*x)) + (m-1)*abs(sin(w*x))), Vp - kk*w*mod(x - T/4, Tp))

steps.explanation: The capacitor is recharged at every peak of the rectified voltage. A half-wave rectifier gives one peak per period $T = 1/f$ = {{T|s}}; a full-wave rectifier gives two, one every $T/2$ = {{T/2|s}}. Measure the distance between successive peaks on the time axis: here it is {{Tp|s}}.

steps.prompt: The graph shows the output of a rectifier with a smoothing capacitor (zoomed in on the top). Read the peak-to-peak ripple voltage $V_r$.

curves.f: max(Vp*((2-m)*max(0, sin(w*x)) + (m-1)*abs(sin(w*x))), Vp - kk*w*mod(x - T/4, Tp))

steps.explanation: The output peaks at {{Vp|V}} each time the capacitor is recharged and sags to {{Vp-Vra|V}} just before the next recharge. $V_r$ = {{Vp|V}} − {{Vp-Vra|V}} = {{Vra|V}}. The average output is about $V_{peak} - V_r/2$ = {{Vp-Vra/2|V}}. Note that the vertical axis does not start at zero.

steps.prompt: This rectifier runs from a {{f}} Hz source and its load draws a practically constant {{IL|A}}. Use the graph to estimate the smoothing capacitance $C$.
steps.hint: You need two readings: how often the capacitor is recharged, and the ripple $V_r$.

curves.f: max(Vp*((2-m)*max(0, sin(w*x)) + (m-1)*abs(sin(w*x))), Vp - kk*w*mod(x - T/4, Tp))

steps.explanation: The peaks are {{Tp|s}} apart (the source period is {{T|s}}: one recharge per period means half-wave, two means full-wave) and the ripple is $V_r$ ≈ {{Vra|V}}. Between recharges the capacitor alone supplies the load, so $C V_r = I_L \times$ {{Tp|s}}: $C$ = {{IL|A}} × {{Tp|s}} / {{Vra|V}} = {{IL*Tp/Vra|F}}.

steps.prompt: A half-wave rectifier with a smoothing capacitor: the dashed curve is the source voltage $v_s$, the solid curve the output $v_o$. What is the diode doing at point P?

curves.f: max(Vp*((2-m)*max(0, sin(w*x)) + (m-1)*abs(sin(w*x))), Vp - kk*w*mod(x - T/4, Tp))

options: It is off: $C$ alone supplies the load
steps.explanation: The diode can only conduct while the source is above the capacitor voltage. That happens during the short intervals just before each peak, where $v_o$ follows the sine. During the long, slow decay $v_s$ is below $v_o$: the diode is reverse biased and the capacitor supplies the load current on its own.

steps.prompt: The graph shows the load voltage of a full-wave rectifier with a resistive load. Find the frequency of the AC source.
steps.explanation: The output repeats every {{1/(2*f)|s}}, but a full-wave rectifier makes **two** humps per source period (one from each half-cycle). So the source period is $T$ = 2 × {{1/(2*f)|s}} = {{1/f|s}} and $f = 1/T$ = {{f|Hz}}. That is also why the ripple of a full-wave rectifier has frequency $2f$.

steps.prompt: A bridge rectifier ($V_m$ = 12 V, 0.7 V diodes, {{f|Hz}}) feeds a load drawing about {{IL|A}}. Choose the smoothing capacitor for a peak-to-peak ripple of {{Vr|V}}.
steps.hint: Between peaks the capacitor supplies $I_L$ for half a period.
steps.explanation:
In a full-wave rectifier the capacitor is recharged every half period, so it supplies the load for $T/2$: $C V_r = I_L T/2$, i.e.
$C = \frac{I_L T}{2V_r}$ = {{IL|A}} × {{T|s}} / (2 × {{Vr|V}}) = **{{Ct|F}}**.
The output peaks at $V_m - 1.4$ = 10.6 V (two diodes conduct) and sags by about {{Vr|V}} before the next peak.
